summary.title: ARCHITECTURE.md
summary.one_liner: Learn why open-source projects of 10k-200k lines should keep a short ARCHITECTURE.md codemap, and how to write one that stays useful over time.
keywords: where is the code that does x
takeaways: Add a short ARCHITECTURE file next to README and CONTRIBUTING in open-source projects of roughly 10k-200k lines of code.
Core developers mainly know the project's physical architecture; the ARCHITECTURE file helps newcomers build that mental map cheaply.
Only document things unlikely to change frequently, keep it short, and revisit it a couple of times a year rather than syncing it with code.
Start with a bird's eye overview, then a coarse-grained codemap answering 'where is the thing that does X?', naming key files and types without direct links.
Call out architectural invariants and layer or system boundaries, then add a separate section on cross-cutting concerns.
summary.summary: The page is matklad's essay arguing that open-source projects in the 10k-200k line range should include an ARCHITECTURE document. It explains the gap between occasional contributors and core developers, which is knowledge of the project's physical layout, and presents the ARCHITECTURE file as a low-effort way to close that gap. It then gives practical guidance: keep it short, change only what rarely changes, start with an overview, write a codemap of coarse modules, name important entities without links, state invariants and boundaries, and finish with cross-cutting concerns. It points to rust-analyzer's architecture document as an example.
